newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmens eye oil revival but export issue sticky.
newsitem.headline: Turkmens eye oil revival but export issue sticky.

text.p: Turkmenistan's oil industry will enjoy a revival as foreign-backed projects develop but faces a dilemma in getting the oil to markets, Western oil executives said on Tuesday.

"I see no reason why production increases from onshore projects shouldn't be 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) or more over the next few years," said Oliver Waldron, president of LEA Ltd, which has a 50-50 offshore joint venture with the Central Asian country.
LEA is 60 percent owned by British-Irish Dragon Oil Plc .
Oil and gas condensate from Turkmenistan's ragged, Soviet-era wells slumped to 3.5 million tonnes (70,000 bpd) in 1995 before recovering to about 5.5 million tonnes (110,000 bpd) in 1996.
Turkmenistan became independent in 1991 but has found the financial break from Moscow hard. It is now pinning its economic hopes on a revival in oil and gas.

The country sits on huge energy reserves. Oil and Gas Industry and Natural Resources Minister Gochmurad Nazdzhanov told an international projects conference these totalled 21 trillion cubic metres of gas and 6.5 billion tonnes of oil.

"A target of about 200,000 bpd onshore is reasonable in the longer term," said Adrian Skelt, consultant at Britain's Monument Oil and Gas Plc, speaking at the conference in the Turkmen capital, Ashgabat.
Monument has an onshore production-sharing agreement with part of Mobil Oil Corp of the United States.
The output rise could accelerate if offshore developments in the Turkmen part of the Caspian Sea get going.
Estimates from U.S. group Unocal Corp put total Turkmen crude oil and condensate production at 600,000 bpd by 2005 and 700,000 bpd by 2010.

Waldron said LEA's joint venture, which is exploiting two fields in Caspian waters, was producing only 7,000 bpd now but planned to boost output to 14-15,000 bpd within 12 months and to 60-80,000 bpd in five years.

Development of offshore Turkmen oil lags well behind that of nearby Caspian rival Azerbaijan, where an international consortium is already working on offshore fields in an $8 billion venture expected to produce 700,000 bpd by 2010.

But Turkmenistan plans to open up its offshore sector with an investment tender, which executives said could be held later this year. Several Western firms have expressed interest in offshore investments but have not yet signed any deals.
Virtually all Turkmenistan's oil output is used in the country. Any rise in output would have to be exported.
"We are looking to expand output," said Brett Majors at Mobil. "But transportation is a problem."

Possible medium-term solutions include selling oil to traders in the Caspian, delivering oil into pipelines planned from the west coast of the Caspian to the Black Sea and selling oil to Iran, possibly as swaps.
"This may seem like bringing coal to Newcastle," Waldron said. "But you save money on transportation by swapping sweet (low sulphur) Turkmen oil for lower-quality Iranian oil in the Persian Gulf."
In the summer, companies may also ship oil along Russian rivers to the Black Sea oil export outlet of Novorossiisk.
A long-term solution might come in the form of a major oil pipeline project aimed at collecting crude from a number of countries bordering the Caspian, including Turkmenistan.
Unocal plans to extend an existing pipeline connecting Siberia with Turkmenistan's Chardzhou oil field to an export terminal on Pakistan's coast via Afghanistan.
The route's capacity is seen at one million bpd, of which Turkmenistan would supply about a tenth of the volume, said Neil Smith, vice-president at Unocal International Ventures Ltd.
"We are hopeful it will be completed within the next five years but it depends on the situation in Afghanistan," he said.
Company officials said the investment environment in Turkmenistan was far from perfect but had improved as the cash-strapped country saw its need for foreign investment.
"Sure, there were start-up problems with moving away from a centrally-controlled economy but it's getting better," Smith said.
A law governing development of hydrocarbon resources was signed recently by the government, further calming investors' jitters, Skelt said.
